cues.zh: 你读那篇论文之前本来就打算做的事。
cues.en: you were going to do before you read that paper.

cues.zh: 所有这些关于底层原理的信息
cues.en: All of this information about what's under the hood

cues.zh: 确实很有趣，也有着各种深远的意义，
cues.en: is interesting and it has all kinds of implications,

cues.zh: 但它唯独不会做的一件事，
cues.en: but the one thing it does not do

cues.zh: 就是减轻你应负的责任——
cues.en: is diminish your responsibility

cues.zh: 去尽可能活出最精彩、最有意义的人生。
cues.en: for living the best, most meaningful life you can.

cues.zh: 它完全不会动摇这一点。
cues.en: It doesn't affect any of that.

cues.zh: 我对此有一种思考角度，
cues.en: And one way I think about this,

cues.zh: 很多科幻作品也探讨过这个话题，
cues.en: and there's lots of sci-fi about this,

cues.zh: 但你或许会记得这么一幕，
cues.en: but one thing that you might remember is,

cues.zh: 你看过电影《机械姬》（Ex Machina）吗？
cues.en: you've seen the film Ex Machina?

cues.zh: 看过。
cues.en: Yes.

cues.zh: 片中有这么一场戏，男主角
cues.en: And so there's one scene there where the protagonist,

cues.zh: 正站在一面镜子前，
cues.en: he's standing in front of a mirror

cues.zh: 整个人彻底吓坏了，
cues.en: and he's completely freaked out

cues.zh: 因为那个 AI 实在太逼真了，
cues.en: because the AI is so lifelike,

cues.zh: 他甚至开始怀疑自己是不是也是个生化机器人。
cues.en: he's now wondering maybe he's a robotic organism too.

cues.zh: 于是他割开自己的手，凝视着自己的眼睛，
cues.en: And so he's cutting his hand and he's looking in his eye

cues.zh: 试图弄清楚自己到底算什么。
cues.en: and he's trying to figure out what he is.

cues.zh: 我们不妨来仔细剖析一下这个场景。
cues.en: And so let's just dissect that for a minute.

cues.zh: 他这么做的原因，
cues.en: The reason he's doing this,

cues.zh: 而大多数人的情况，
cues.en: and what happens to most people,

cues.zh: 我觉得这挺有意思的，
cues.en: which I think is quite interesting,

cues.zh: 就是如果他们打开自己的手臂
cues.en: is that if they were to open their arm

cues.zh: 发现里面有一堆齿轮和机械结构，
cues.en: and they find a bunch of cogs and gears inside,

cues.zh: 我觉得大多数人会非常沮丧
cues.en: I think most people would be super depressed

cues.zh: 因为我觉得大多数人会这样想，
cues.en: because I think where most people go with this is,

cues.zh: 我刚刚了解到了关于自己的某些真相。
cues.en: I've just learned something about myself.

cues.zh: 意思是，我知道齿轮和机械结构能做什么，它们是一台机器，而我刚刚发现自己满身都是齿轮和机械结构，所以我不再是我以为的那个自己了。
cues.en: Meaning, I know what cogs and gears can do, they're a machine, and I just learned that I'm full of cogs and gears, therefore I'm not what I thought I was.

cues.zh: 我觉得这种想法真的很不幸，因为你的意思是，你整个人生的体验、所有的快乐与痛苦、个人责任以及你经历的一切，
cues.en: And I think this is a really unfortunate way to think because what you're saying is, your experience of your whole life and all of the joys and the suffering and the personal responsibility and everything else that you've experienced,

cues.zh: 你现在愿意把这一切都放弃，就因为你觉得你了解了齿轮和机械结构能做什么。
cues.en: you're now willing to give all that up because you think you know something about what cogs and gears can do.

cues.zh: 我会往完全相反的方向想：太棒了，我刚发现齿轮和传动装置竟然能做到这么不可思议的事。
cues.en: I would go in the exact opposite direction and I would say, amazing, I've just discovered that cogs and gears can do this incredible thing.

cues.zh: 哇，为什么不呢？你觉得，为什么蛋白质、离子，还有你体内的各种蛋白质和其他物质，就能实现真正的认知？
cues.en: Like, wow. And why not? Because why do you think that proteins and the ions and proteins and the various things in your body, those are great for true cognition?

cues.zh: 我一直知道自己浑身都是蛋白质、脂质和离子之类的东西，我觉得这挺酷，也能接受自己是这种机器。但齿轮和传动装置？绝不可能。
cues.en: Like, I always knew I was full of protein and lipids and ions and all of those things, and that was cool, I was okay with being that kind of machine, but cogs and gears? No way.

cues.zh: 所以我觉得，专注于某些唯物主义观点的教育，让我们对不同材料能做到什么产生了毫无根据的自信。
cues.en: And so I think one thing that we get from our education focused on certain kinds of materialism is that we get this unwarranted confidence in what we think different materials are capable of.

cues.zh: 而且我们对此深信不疑。我觉得这作为一种教育或社会现象，实在令人惊讶：我们如此彻底地接受了这种说法，甚至愿意放弃自己对自身的一切了解，只为了坚持一种关于材料的说法。
cues.en: And we believe it to such an extent, I mean, I find this amazing as a kind of an educational or sociological thing that we imbibe that story so strongly that we're willing to then give up everything that we know about ourselves in order to stick to a story about materials.

cues.zh: 我觉得笛卡尔有一点说得非常非常对：你真正确知的一件事，就是你是一个有责任、有心智、有各种潜能的主体存在，而你学到的一切都建立在这个基础之上。
cues.en: I think that's one thing that I think Descartes had really, really right, is that the one thing you actually know is that you are an agentic being with responsibility and a mind and all this potential, and whatever you learn is on the background of that.

cues.zh: 所以如果你发现自己是由齿轮和发条组成的，你该得出的结论只是：太好了，现在我知道这些东西也能像蛋白质一样做到。所以我真正希望人们从中得到的，就是这个简单的想法：关于硬件的任何发现，关于其生物学或物理学的任何发现，都不该让你偏离你存在的根本现实。
cues.en: So if you find out that you are made of cogs and gears, all you should conclude is, well, great. Now I know this stuff can do it as well as proteins can. And so what I really hope that people get from this is simply the idea that pretty much no discovery about the hardware, no discovery about the biology or the physics of it should pull you away from the fundamental reality of your being.

cues.zh: 无论你到底是什么，你知道，是一群细胞，还是从柏拉图空间里拉下来的涌现心智，或者别的什么，不管哪种说法正确，归根结底，你仍然是那个惊人的、整合的存在，拥有潜能，也有去行动的责任。
cues.en: That whatever it is that you are, you know, groups of cells, an emergent mind pulled down from platonic space or whatever, whichever of these things are correct, the bottom line is you are still the amazing integrated being with potential and a responsibility to do things.

cues.zh: 哈。很多人不喜欢唯物主义，喜欢他们认为是非唯物主义的东西，可能是唯心主义、灵性主义，随便他们怎么叫，或者非二元论，或者三元论而不是二元论。他们部分上是在说，看，我不是物质的，因为他们贬低物质，把物质看成机械的、没有生命的。
cues.en: Aha. So many people who dislike materialism and like the more whatever they consider to be not materialism, so it could be idealism, it could be spiritualism or whatever they want to call it, or non-dualism, or trialism instead of a dualism, in part what they're saying is, look, I'm not material because they denigrate the material and they view it as robotic, lifeless.

cues.zh: 但你说还有另一条路，如果你是物质的，不管最终你是什么，你可以提升它。所以你可以说，看，它有一种活力，有一种旺盛，有一种超越生命的东西，在我之前认为僵化的东西里。
cues.en: But you're saying there's another route, if you are material, whatever it is you turn out to be, you can elevate that. So you can say, look, there's a dynamism to it, there's an exuberance, there's a larger-than-lifeness to what I previously thought was ossifying.

cues.zh: 是的，当然。伊恩·麦克吉尔克里斯特也强调了这一点，他说我们低估了物质。你知道，当我们谈论唯物主义时，我们一直被灌输并且仍在灌输这种观念：物质缺乏智能。
cues.en: Yeah, for sure. And Ian McGilchrist makes a point of this too, he says that we've underestimated matter. You know, when we talk about materialism, we have been sold and are selling still this notion of matter as lacking intelligence.

cues.zh: 我觉得我们不该盲目自信，自以为很清楚物质能做到什么。我们在极度简易的系统中，都发现了全新的原始认知能力，真的是极简系统。这些发现总让我们感到惊讶，甚至震撼。
cues.en: And I think that we need to give up this unwarranted confidence in what we think matter can do. We are finding novel proto-cognitive capacities in extremely minimal systems, extremely minimal systems. And they're surprising to us, they're shocking when we find these things.

cues.zh: 我认为我们很不擅长辨别哪些系统能孕育出心智。所以如果觉得“我们不过是某种特定系统，这种系统绝不可能拥有崇高能动性”，进而感到沮丧，那真的为时过早了。
cues.en: And I think we are really bad at recognizing what kinds of systems can give rise to minds, and therefore being depressed because we think that we are a particular kind of system and there's no way that system can be this majestic, agentic being, it's way too early for that.

cues.zh: 我们就是——我是说，最关键的问题之一在于，我们总自以为知道各种物质能做什么。显然，我指的不仅是均匀单一的材料块，而是指特定的组织结构。
cues.en: We just, we absolutely, I mean, this is one of the, I think, the major things is that we have this idea that we know what different kinds of matter can do. And obviously, I'm not just talking about, you know, homogenous blocks of material, I'm talking about specific configurations.

cues.zh: 但极简的事物也可能具备非常惊人的认知特性。所以说，现在就认为我们搞懂了这里面的机制，还为时过早。
cues.en: But really minimal kinds of things can have some very surprising cognitive qualities. And so, yeah, it's way too early to think that we know what's going on here.

cues.zh: 我们这儿录了大概45分钟了，居然一次都没提过“生物电”这个词。所以，给你点个赞，也给我点个赞，这到底是怎么做到的，迈克·莱文的访谈里竟然没提生物电。那么生物电跟这些到底有什么关系？
cues.en: I think we have a record here of 45 minutes of recording or so, and we haven't mentioned the word bioelectricity once. So, kudos to you, kudos to me, how the heck did that happen, for a Mike Levin interview. So what does bioelectricity have to do with any of this?

cues.zh: 对，生物电并不神奇，它也不是独一无二的，因为宇宙中很可能还有其他方式能实现它的功能。但生物电在地球生命形式中所起的作用非常有意思。它就像一种认知胶水。
cues.en: Yeah, so bioelectricity is not magic, it is not unique in the sense that there are probably, this is certainly out in the universe, there are probably other ways of doing what it does. But what it does here on Earth in living forms is something very interesting. It functions as a kind of cognitive glue.

cues.zh: 所以，当面对集体智能时，你需要制定策略和机制，让有能力的个体能够融合为一个更大的涌现个体，并实现几件事。
cues.en: So, when you have collective intelligence, you need to have policies and you need to have mechanisms for enabling competent individuals to merge together into a larger emergent individual that's going to do several things.

cues.zh: 首先，更高层级的庞大网络会改变底层层级的选择空间。虽然各部分仍在做自己该做的事，但它们现在的运作方式与全局的高层叙事和高阶目标保持了一致，因为它们的行动空间被更高层级弯曲、重塑了。它们的感知和能量空间也同样被重塑了。
cues.en: First of all, the larger network, the larger level is going to distort the option space for the lower levels. So the parts are doing things that the parts do, but they're now doing it in a way that is coherent with a much higher level story of what's going on, higher level goals, because their action landscape is bent, it's distorted by the larger level. Their perception, their energy landscape is distorted.

cues.zh: 因此，这个集体——这个全新的自我——将拥有记忆、目标、偏好以及认知视界。这需要一些非常特定的特质，而且有很多。而促成这一切、让认知视界扩展、让智能得以扩展的途径之一，就是生物电。
cues.en: So that collective is going to, that new self, is going to have memories, goals, preferences, a cognitive lico. That requires some very specific features, and there are a bunch of them. And one of the modalities that lets that happen, that lets the cognitive lico scale, that lets the intelligence scale, is bioelectricity.

cues.zh: 所以，通过让细胞融入电网络，会产生一些非常有趣的宏观动态——当然，我们在人工神经网络中利用的也是这一点，对吧？这就是生物学。从细菌生物膜时代开始你就能发现，电信号是涌现出更高层级细胞和更高级计算的绝佳途径。可能还有其他实现方式，但在地球上，生物电往往是最优解。
cues.en: So by taking cells and enabling them to be part of an electrical network, there are some really interesting larger level dynamics, which, you know, this is what we exploit in artificial neural networks, of course, right? This is biology. You notice this since the time of bacterial biofilms, that electricity is just a really good way for higher level cells to emerge and higher level computation to emerge. There are probably other ways of doing it, but here on Earth, bioelectricity tends to be the way to go.

cues.zh: 在探讨“高阶自我”、“低阶自我”或“更高目标”的对话中，我总在思考一个问题：我们究竟如何去界定所谓的“高”或“低”？尤其是当我们讨论的是高维空间中如此广袤的目标图景或认知轨迹，而实数轴是唯一具有全序关系的连续统一体。
cues.en: Something I always wonder in conversations about are higher selves, lower selves, higher goals. How do we even say higher or lower, when what we're talking about is such a vast landscape of goals or cognitive lico in a higher dimensional space, where the real number line is the only continuum that has an ordering to it.

cues.zh: 一旦引入复数，或者 R2、R3 等高维空间，你就无法直接挑出两个点说哪个“更高”，除非你引入额外的结构。那么，究竟是什么让我们能评判高低呢？
cues.en: As soon as you have the complex numbers, or R2 or R3, etc., you can't pick two points and say one is higher than another, unless you implement other structure. So what is it that allows us to say higher or lower?

cues.zh: 这是用词不当，你说得完全没错。这里唯一关键的在于——因为更高一级并不一定比低级更聪明，通常可能如此，但绝非必然。在物理尺度上也不一定更大或更小。
cues.en: Bad vocabulary. You're 100% right. The only thing that matters here, because it doesn't necessarily mean the next level up is not necessarily smarter than the lower level, usually, but that doesn't guarantee that at all. Not necessarily bigger or smaller in physical scale.

cues.zh: 对于这些概念，我们确实还缺乏一套精准的词汇。但我所说的“更高”，指的其实类似集合的隶属关系。仅仅是像组织由细胞构成、细胞由分子网络构成这样的事实。仅此而已，我指的就只有这个。我并不是说它更大、更聪明或更有价值。我只是说，在这种异质分层结构中，某些事物是由另一些事物构成的。仅此而已，这就是我的全部意思。
cues.en: We really don't have a great vocabulary yet for all this stuff, but the only thing I mean by higher is something akin to set membership. Just the fact that a tissue is made up of cells, and cells are made up of molecular networks. That's it. That's all I'm talking about. I'm not saying that it's bigger or more intelligent or more valuable. All I mean is that in this heterarchy, certain things are made up of other things. That's it. That's all I mean.

cues.zh: 之前定义智能时，我记得你提过威廉·詹姆斯说的不仅涉及能力，还涉及手段。也就是为单一目标生成多种路径的能力。我不知道是否也包含设定多个目标的能力，我们可以探讨一下。但假设选定一个目标，你能为它生成多种路径，有多种执行方式。但我记得你还提到了手段。对吧？
cues.en: Earlier when defining intelligence, I believe you said William James's was something about ability, but also means. So ability to generate multiple paths to a single goal. I don't know if it was also the ability to have multiple goals, but we can explore that. But let's pick out a goal, then you can generate multiple paths to that goal, many ways of executing. But then you also, I believe you said the means to as well. Is that correct?

cues.zh: 对吧？没错，在詹姆斯的语境里，至少按我的理解，他说的手段其实就是指路径。那就是路径。所谓通往目标的手段，对吧？就是带你达成目标的路径。我们在生物学中经常看到这种现象。举个例子，大家听到我谈论发育智能之类的概念时，往往会以为我指的是复杂度。
cues.en: Is that correct? Yeah, the means in James's, at least the way I read him, when he says means, he means the path. That is the path. A means to an end, right? It's a path that takes you to that end. So this is the kind of stuff we see in biology. Just to give you an example, one thing that people often think when they hear me talk about the intelligence of development and so on, people often think I mean the complexity.

cues.zh: 仅仅是从一颗受精卵开始，最终变成一只蝾螈什么的，复杂度确实增加了。人们很自然地会想，这不过是简单规则演化出复杂结果的常见例子嘛。那只是涌现出来的复杂性，并不是智能。他们说得没错，我指的也不是这个，那确实不算智能。
cues.en: Just the fact that you start from an egg and you end up with, I don't know, a salamander or something, that there's an increase in complexity. And then rightly, people think, well, that's just, you know, there's lots of examples where simple rules give rise to complex outcomes. That's just emergent complexity. That's not intelligence. And they're right. That is not what I mean. That's not intelligence.

cues.zh: 我所说的智能，是指解决以下这类问题的能力。比方说，
cues.en: What I mean by intelligence is the problem solving of the following kind. So let's say

cues.zh: 你有一颗蝾螈的卵。你可以玩这么一个把戏：
cues.en: you have an egg belonging to a salamander. One of the tricks you can do is prevent it

cues.zh: 在遗传物质复制时阻止细胞分裂。这样你就会得到多倍体的
cues.en: from dividing while the genetic material is copying. And so you end up with polyploid

cues.zh: 蝾螈。所以不再是2n，而是4n、5n、6n、8n之类的。那么，
cues.en: newts. So instead of 2n, you can have 4n, 5n, 6n, 8n, that kind of thing. Well, what

cues.zh: 这样做会发生什么呢？细胞会变大以容纳
cues.en: happens when you do that, what happens is the cells get bigger in order to accommodate

cues.zh: 多出来的遗传物质，但蝾螈本身的体型却保持不变。所以如果你
cues.en: the extra genetic material, but the actual salamander stays the same size. So if you

cues.zh: 切一个横截面，比如我们切一根通向肾脏的微小肾小管的
cues.en: take a cross-section, so let's say we take a cross-section of a little tubule, a kidney

cues.zh: 横截面。正常情况下，大概是由8到10个小细胞
cues.en: tubule, that runs to the kidneys. Normally, there's like 8 to 10 little cells that go

cues.zh: 围成一圈构成这根小管，中间是管腔。所以如果你把
cues.en: in a circle to make that tubule, and then there's a lumen in the middle. So if you make

cues.zh: 细胞变得巨大，你首先会注意到，首先，拥有多倍体
cues.en: the cells gigantic, the first thing you notice is that, well, first of all, having multiple

cues.zh: 一份遗传物质的拷贝，你依然能得到一只正常的蝾螈。所以这真是相当惊人
cues.en: copies of the genetic material, you still get a normal newt. So that's pretty amazing

cues.zh: 已经。第二件惊人的事是，当细胞随遗传物质的数量缩放时，
cues.en: already. Second amazing thing is when the cells scale to the amount of genetic material,

cues.zh: 也就是细胞变大。这很惊人。然后你会发现，其实，既然
cues.en: so the cells get larger. That's amazing. Then you find that, well, actually, since

cues.zh: 细胞非常大，现在只有少数几个细胞协同工作，来构成完全
cues.en: the cells are really big, only a few of them are now working together to make the exact

cues.zh: 同样大小的肾小管。所以它们缩放细胞数量，来弥补细胞尺寸的异常，
cues.en: same size tubule. So they scale the number of cells to make up for the aberrant size

cues.zh: 对吧？这说得通吧？然后最惊人的事情发生了，
cues.en: of the cell, right? That makes sense? And then the most amazing thing of all happens

cues.zh: 当你制造出真正巨大的细胞时，甚至没有空间容纳超过一个。一个细胞
cues.en: when you make truly gigantic cells, there's not even room for more than one. One cell

cues.zh: 会自身弯折，在中间留下一个腔。这之所以惊人，是因为
cues.en: will bend around itself, leaving a lumen in the middle. The reason that's amazing is that

cues.zh: 那需要一种不同的分子机制。那是细胞骨架的弯折，而之前
cues.en: that requires a different molecular mechanism. That's cytoskeletal bending, whereas before

cues.zh: 你用的是细胞间的通讯。所以就是这类事情，对吧？所以只要

cues.en: And by the way, there was that eye spot, which, which is, which is why the eye thing worked.

cues.zh: 我们成功证实了，各种导致面部发育畸形的先天缺陷，都是通过抑制正常的生物电模式造成的，而且这种缺陷是可以被修复的。
cues.en: And we were able to show that all kinds of birth defects that mess up the formation of face, do it by, uh, uh, uh, inhibiting the normal bioelectric pattern and that you could fix it.

cues.zh: 也就是说，你可以通过这种方式来实现修复效果。
cues.en: You know, you could, you could, you could, um, exert, um, repair effects that way.

cues.zh: 所以，嗯，这个发现非常有趣。
cues.en: So, uh, so that was, uh, so that was, that was interesting.

cues.zh: 后来，我们开始研究再生，早期工作同样是由 Danny 完成的。
cues.en: Then, then we, when we started looking at regeneration, um, and again, the early work was done also by Danny.

cues.zh: 之后则是由 Kelly Chang 接手，她现在是内华达大学拉斯维加斯分校的教职人员；当时我们的工作证实了，蝌蚪尾部的再生同样是由生物电驱动的。
cues.en: And then later on by Kelly Chang, who's now a faculty member at university of Las Vegas, where what we did was, uh, we showed that, um, tadpole tail regeneration was also bioelectrically driven.

cues.zh: 那是我们在再生领域首次实现“功能获得”效果，证明了我们确实可以诱导全新的再生过程。
cues.en: And that was our first gain of function, uh, effect in regeneration, where we are able to show that we could actually induce new regeneration.

cues.zh: 尾巴其实是一个非常复杂的器官。
cues.en: So the tail is a very complex organ.

cues.zh: 它有脊髓、肌肉、骨骼，好吧，没有骨骼，有脉管系统、神经分布、外周神经以及皮肤。
cues.en: It has a spinal cord, muscle, bone, well, not bone, vasculature, um, uh, innervation, um, peripheral innervation, skin.

cues.zh: 所以，我们选用了通常不能再生的蝌蚪，它们在某个发育阶段是无法再生尾巴的。
cues.en: And so, um, we took, we took tadpoles that normally do not regenerate and there's a, there's a stage at which they, they can't regenerate their tails.

cues.zh: 我们研发了一种生物电混合制剂，可以诱导它重新生长。
cues.en: And we developed a bioelectric cocktail that induces it to, to grow.

cues.zh: 我当时的博士后 Kelly Chang 说：“我把它们浸泡了一下。”我就问：“那你泡了多久？”
cues.en: My, my, my, my postdoc at the time, Kelly Chang said, um, I, I, I soaked them and I said, well, how long did you, how long did you soak them for?

cues.zh: 她说泡了一个小时。
cues.en: And she said an hour.

cues.zh: 我心想，这时间肯定太短了。
cues.en: And I thought, I felt, but that's gotta be too short.

cues.zh: 泡一个小时绝对不可能起作用。
cues.en: There's no way an hour soak is going to do anything.

cues.zh: 然而事实证明，正是这一个小时的浸泡，引发了后续长达八天的再生过程，期间我们完全没有进行任何干预。
cues.en: And sure enough, that, that hour soak led to, uh, eight days of regeneration where we don't touch it at all.

cues.zh: 这项工作最新的版本在蛙腿实验中，我们展示了用我们的混合剂刺激24小时，就能诱导出一年半的腿部生长，而在这段时间里我们完全不去碰它。
cues.en: And the most recent version of that work is in the frog leg, where we show that 24 hour stimulation with our cocktail induces a year and a half of leg growth during which time we don't touch it at all.

cues.zh: 所以令人惊叹的 again 是，这不是微观管理。
cues.en: So the amazing thing there is again, this is not micromanagement.

cues.zh: 这不是3D打印。
cues.en: This is not 3d printing.

cues.zh: 这不是我们在这不可思议的一年半过程中告诉每个细胞该去哪里。
cues.en: This is not us telling every cell where to go during this incredible year and a half long process.

cues.zh: 这是在最早的时刻，你传达给细胞：走建腿的路径，而不是疤痕的路径。
cues.en: This is at the very earliest moment you communicate to the cells, go down the leg building path, not the scarring path.

cues.zh: 就这样。
cues.en: And that's it.

cues.zh: 然后你就放手不管了。
cues.en: And then you take your hands off.

cues.zh: 这，这，这就像是调用一个子程序。
cues.en: It's, it's, it's calling a subroutine.

cues.zh: 这是模块化。
cues.en: It's modularity.

cues.zh: 这是依靠材料的自身能力，你不需要去微观管理它。
cues.en: It's relying on the competency of the, of the material where you're not going to micromanage it.

cues.zh: 那是我们第一次明确意识到这是可能的，当时她证明了，只需对
cues.en: So that was, so that was the first time that kind of became obvious that that was possible is when, when she, she showed that an hour, um, just an hour stimulation of the

cues.zh: 正确的生物电状态进行短短一小时的刺激，就能促使整个尾巴开始自主再生。
cues.en: correct bioelectrical state got the whole tail to commit to regenerate itself.

cues.zh: 那是我们再生研究项目的开端，之后我们转向了四肢，而现在，我们正努力推进到
cues.en: Uh, so that was, that was the beginning of our regeneration program after which we went into limbs and, uh, and, and, uh, now of course we're trying to push into, into

cues.zh: 哺乳动物的肢体上。
cues.en: mammalian, you know, into mammalian limbs.

cues.zh: 在这过程中，Celia Herrera-Rincon 和 Naroshi Murugan 等其他博士后，也展示了青蛙等动物的腿部再生。
cues.en: Um, yeah, along, along the, along the way, uh, Celia Herrera-Rincon and, uh, Naroshi Murugan were other postdocs that, uh, that, that showed leg regeneration in frog and so on.

cues.zh: 大约在那个时期，我非常想研究癌症，非常想探索癌症中存在生物电因素这个构想。
cues.en: Um, around, around that time we had, uh, we had another thing we, we really, I really wanted to work on cancer and I really wanted to work on this, um, on this idea that, uh, there's a bioelectric component to it.

cues.zh: 你可以这样想：问题不是为什么会有癌症，而是为什么会有不是癌症的东西？
cues.en: And, and the, and the way you can, you can think about it is simply that not why is there cancer, but why is there anything but cancer?

cues.zh: 那么，细胞为什么会合作，而不是都变成变形虫？
cues.en: So, so why do cells ever cooperate instead of being amoebas?

cues.zh: 它们为什么会合作？
cues.en: Why do they ever cooperate?

cues.zh: 我们知道，生物电信号就像一种认知胶水，把它们凝聚起来，共同完成大规模的建造工程，比如维持器官的运作。
cues.en: And so we know that the bioelectric signaling is the kind of, um, cognitive glue that, that binds them together towards these large scale construction projects, maintaining organs and things like that.

cues.zh: 所以，我们想从生物电的角度来研究这个问题。
cues.en: And so, um, yeah, so we wanted to study that bioelectrically.

cues.zh: 我有两位学生，Brooke Cherinette 和 Maria Labikin，承担了这项研究。
cues.en: And so I had, I had two students, uh, Brooke Cherinette and, uh, Maria Labikin who, uh, undertook that.

cues.zh: 我们用生物电成像发现，可以提前判断哪些细胞会发生转化。
cues.en: And we were able to show that using this bioelectrical imaging, you can tell which cells were going to convert ahead of time.

cues.zh: 你甚至可以通过给完全正常的细胞传递错误的环境生物电信号，让它们变成转移性黑色素瘤。
cues.en: You could also convince perfectly normal cells to become metastatic melanoma just by giving them inappropriate bioelectric cues about their environment.

cues.zh: 所以你可以，你知道，没有基因损伤，没有致癌物，也没有癌基因，只是生物电信息出了错，它们就会变得像转移性黑色素瘤。
cues.en: So you can, you can know, no, no genetic damage, no carcinogens, no oncogenes, but, but just the wrong bioelectric information and they become like metastatic melanoma.

cues.zh: 嗯，最棒的是，他们证明了，通过与邻近细胞建立适当的生物电连接，实际上可以逆转——不是逆转——嗯，致癌刺激，比如人类癌基因的影响。
cues.en: Um, and, and best of all, they were able to show that you can actually reverse, not reverse, um, carcinogenic stimuli, for example, human oncogenes by appropriate bioelectric connections to their neighbors.

cues.zh: 所以我们有一系列论文，嗯，展示了如何通过生物电来控制细胞。
cues.en: So we had a whole set of, uh, we had a whole set of papers, um, showing how to, uh, how to control, uh, cells bioelectrically.

cues.zh: 现在，我实验室的 Juanita Matthews 正在研究如何把这些策略应用到人类癌症上。
cues.en: And, uh, uh, Juanita Matthews in my lab now is tracking to take, um, take all those strategies into human, into human cancer.

cues.zh: 所以这是 2009 年？
cues.en: So this is 2009?

cues.zh: 是的，最早的实验大概是在 2010 年、2011 年左右做的。
cues.en: This was, yeah, the first, the, the first experiments were, were done around, um, 2010, 2011, something like that.

cues.zh: 你是什么时候想到生物电与癌症之间可能存在联系的？
cues.en: So when did this conjectural connection between bioelectricity and cancer occur to you?

cues.zh: 当时这个领域对此一无所知。
cues.en: The field was clueless about that.

cues.zh: 他们不是有看法之后明确说不。
cues.en: It's not as if they had an opinion and said no.

cues.zh: 嗯，说清楚一点，最早谈到这件事的人是 Clarence Cohn，他在 1971 年就提过。
cues.en: Well, uh, to, to be, to be, to be clear, the very first person who talked about this was Clarence Cohn in 1971.

cues.zh: 1971 年，Clarence Cohn 在《Science》上发表了几篇论文，指出细胞的静息电位是推动细胞增殖的重要因素。
cues.en: So Clarence Cohn in 71 wrote that, uh, he had a couple of papers, uh, in, in, in science where he showed that, uh, resting potential of cells was an important, um, driver of cell proliferation.

cues.zh: 他还推测这可能和癌症有关。
cues.en: And he conjectured that it might have something to do with, with, with cancer.

cues.zh: 所以这个想法当时已经有人提出来了。
cues.en: So this idea had been floated.

cues.zh: 以前从来没人研究过它。
cues.en: Nobody had ever done anything with it.

cues.zh: 而且，呃，直到我们造出这些工具，大家才有办法在分子层面研究它。
cues.en: And, and, and they, and the, uh, tools to study this at a molecular level didn't exist until, until we made them.

cues.zh: 你知道，生物电对癌症很重要这个想法，以前就有了。
cues.en: So, you know, that, that idea, just, just that bioelectricity is important in cancer had been around before.

cues.zh: 嗯，我认为我们带来的全新观点是：这也与认知有关。
cues.en: Um, what I think we brought to it that was completely new is the notion of that this is also related to cognition.

cues.zh: 这个想法是，它不只是推动细胞增殖和癌症；它还参与设定认知光锥的大小上限。到了那个阶段，细胞会获得古老的、类似转移的行为方式，就像变形虫那样。我认为，这一层面是我们全新的发现。
cues.en: The idea that it's not just that it drives proliferation and cancer, that this is really involved in setting the, limiting the size of the cognitive light cone, at which point cells acquire ancient, uh, you know, um, uh, metastatic like behavior, the way that, um, you know, amoebas do, um, that, that aspect of it, I think is, is completely new with us.

cues.zh: 这种关于“这其实关乎自我边界”的想法，我以前从未见其他人讨论过。
cues.en: That, that, that idea that, uh, that this really is about the boundaries of the self, you know, and I've never seen anybody else talk about that.

cues.zh: 大约在同一时期，2009年还发生了一件有趣的事，当时我们正在研究涡虫，也就是扁形虫。
cues.en: So, um, so those, you know, those, those around that same time, there's something else interesting that happened in 2009, which is that we were, we were studying planaria, we were studying flatworms.

cues.zh: 我们已经证实，当你把涡虫切成碎片后，这些碎片决定自己会长出几个头的方式，其实与细胞利用间隙连接进行相互通信的能力有关。
cues.en: Um, and, uh, we had, uh, we had shown that when you cut planaria into pieces, the way that they, these pieces decide how many heads they were going to have, uh, is actually related to the ability of cells to communicate with each other using gap junctions.

cues.zh: 也就是这些电突触。
cues.en: These, these electrical synapses.

cues.zh: 所以当时我们已经培育出了一些双头虫等等。
cues.en: And so we had made some two headed worms and so on.

cues.zh: 大概在2009年左右，我带了一位来自波士顿大学（BU）的访问学者，她叫 Larissa。
cues.en: Um, and, uh, around two, 2009, um, I had this, um, had this, uh, student, this visiting student from BU, her name was Larissa.

cues.zh: 然后，呃，她，她，我们，我让她重新切割双头蠕虫，只用清水，不再，不再进行任何形式的干预。
cues.en: And, uh, she, she, we, I asked her to recut the two headed worms and just in plain water, no more, no more manipulation of any kind.

cues.zh: 我们，我们。
cues.en: We, we.

cues.en: Again.

cues.zh: 对。所以，所以你有一条正常的单头蠕虫，你切掉头和尾，得到中间片段，你，呃，把那个中间片段浸泡在一种药物里，这种药物阻断细胞之间的电信号交流，然后它们两端都长出头来。
cues.en: Yeah. So, so, so you have a normal one headed worm, you cut off the head and the tail, you have the middle fragment, you, uh, soak that middle fragment in a drug that blocks the cells from electrically communicating with each other and they develop heads at both ends.

cues.en: It was a single, one single chemical.

cues.zh: 它，它真的很简单。
cues.en: It was, it was really simple.

cues.zh: 它只是一种，一种单一化学物质，它所做的就是阻断间隙连接。
cues.en: It was just one, one single chemical and all it does is block gap junctions.

cues.zh: 于是，它改变的是电路，呃，细胞所具有的特性，然后它们都，而且，两个伤口都决定它们必须是头部。
cues.en: And so, and so what, what that did was change the electric circuit, uh, properties that, that the cells have and they all, and, and both wounds decided they had to be heads.

cues.zh: 于是现在你就得到了这些双头蠕虫。
cues.en: So now you get these two headed worms.

cues.zh: 于是，是的，Larissa 把这些双头蠕虫放在普通水中重新切割，不再做任何处理，然后她得到了更多双头蠕虫。
cues.en: So, so yeah, so, so Larissa, um, recuts these two headed worms in plain water, no more manipulation and she gets more two headed worms.

cues.en: A penetrance just means that, um, when you apply some treatment to a population, not all of them have an effect and not all of them have the same effect.

cues.zh: 所以多年来我们一直管它们叫幸存者，然后大约在 2015 年，Fallon 加入实验室后，她重新切割了其中一些单头的幸存者，发现它们同样呈现出 70 比 30 的比例，即 70% 变成了双头，30% 没有。
cues.en: So, um, so for years we called them escapees and then, um, uh, around 2015 when Fallon joined the lab, she recut some of those one-headed escapees and found that they also do 70-30, that 70% of them became double-headed and 30% didn't.

cues.zh: 所以我们意识到，它们其实并不是逃脱者，也不是不受影响，它们确实受到了影响，只是受影响的方式很不一样。
cues.en: And so what we realized was that they're not actually escapees, they're not unaffected, they're affected, but the way they're affected is quite different.

cues.zh: 它们是随机化的。
cues.en: They are randomized.

cues.zh: 它们分不清自己该长一个头还是两个头，在每一代里，它们就像抛硬币一样决定该怎么做，概率大约是七三开。
cues.en: They can't tell if they should be one-headed or two-headed and they flip a coin set with a 70-30 bias about what they should do in any given generation.

cues.zh: 事实上，我们能够证明，当你从同一条蠕虫上切下多段时——我们称之为隐性蠕虫，之所以叫隐性，是因为它们外表看起来完全正常，一个头、一条尾，看着正常，但其实并不正常。
cues.en: In fact, we were able to show that when you cut multiple pieces from the same worm, and we call them cryptic worms, cryptic because physically they look completely normal, one head, one tail, they look normal, but they're not normal.

cues.zh: 而且，因为如果再切它们，它们就不知道该怎么了。
cues.en: And, and because, because if you recut them, they're not sure what to do.

cues.zh: 它们的记忆是双稳态的。

cues.zh: 所以情况是，你可以把它们切成多段，每一段都会自己决定是长一个头还是两个头，尽管它们来自同一个母体，频率也大致是同样的七三开。
cues.en: So what happens is that you can cut them into pieces and every piece makes its own decision if it's going to be one-headed or two-headed, even though they came from the same, you know, the same parent organism, uh, with the same roughly 70-30, um, frequency.

cues.zh: 所以，这也是另一种具有持久性的系谱。
